title: Inverse trigonometric functions and principal branches
terms: arcsine; arccosine; arctangent; arccosecant; arcsecant; arccotangent; principal branch; inverse trigonometric function.

exposition.text:
Inverse trig functions invert injective restrictions of the periodic functions. The principal ranges
used here are arcsin x ∈ [−π/2, π/2], arccos x ∈ [0, π], and arctan x ∈ (−π/2, π/2). Their
domains are [−1, 1], [−1, 1], and R, respectively. Thus arcsin(sin x) is not always x; it is the
unique principal angle with the same sine.
We use arccot x ∈ (0, π), arcsec x ∈ [0, π] \ {π/2}, and arccsc x ∈ [−π/2, π/2] \ {0}. The last
two require |x| ≥ 1. Conventions can vary, especially for arccotangent, so specify them. To
simplify compositions, set the inverse expression equal to an angle, recover its other trig values,
and track its quadrant before identifying any sum of angles.

question.text:
What is arcsin(sin(7π/6)) + arccos(cos(5π/3))?
(A) −π/2 (B) −π/6 (C) π/6 (D) π/2 (E) 3π/2

solution.text:
The first principal value is −π/6, since the sine is −1/2. The second is π/3, since the
cosine is 1/2. Their sum is π/6.

question.text:
What is arctan 2 + arctan 3 − arctan(1/5)?
(A) arctan(4/5) (B) π/2 (C) π − arctan(3/2) (D) π + arctan(3/2) (E) 3π/4

solution.text:
Let A = arctan 2 + arctan 3 = 3π/4, since its tangent is −1 and A ∈ (π/2, π). Then
tan(A − arctan(1/5)) = (−1 − 1/5)/(1 − 1/5) = −3/2. The angle remains in quadrant II, so
its principal expression is π − arctan(3/2).

question.text:
With the principal branches stated above, what is arcsec(−2) + arccsc(−2)?
(A) −π/2 (B) π/6 (C) π/2 (D) 5π/6 (E) 7π/6

solution.text:
The principal secant inverse lies in [0, π] \ {π/2}, so arcsec(−2) = 2π/3. The cosecant inverse
lies in [−π/2, π/2] \ {0}, so arccsc(−2) = −π/6. Their sum is π/2.

question.text:
For real x, which identity holds under the convention arccot x ∈ (0, π)?
(A) arccot x = arctan(1/x) for every x ̸= 0
(B) arccot x = π/2 − arctan x
(C) arccot(−x) = − arccot x
(D) arccot x = π/2 + arctan x
(E) arccot x is undefined at x = 0

solution.text:
If u = arctan x ∈ (−π/2, π/2), then π/2−u ∈ (0, π) and its cotangent is tan u = x. Therefore
it is the specified inverse. In particular arccot 0 = π/2, and using arctan(1/x) alone fails for
negative x.
